Ethernet and WiFi access describe how end systems (hosts) attach to LANs and hotspots, so the concept of an end system must come first.

End-to-end delay is defined as the accumulation of nodal delays along the path, so the nodal delay components and formula must be understood first.

The bottleneck-link model and the file-transfer-time approximation F/min{Rs, Rc} rely on the transmission-rate/transmission-delay concept, and its stated caveats (ignoring store-and-forward and processing delays) require knowing those nodal delay components.
Queuing delay is one of the four nodal delay components introduced here; the deep-dive on dqueue presupposes the dnodal = dproc + dqueue + dtrans + dprop framework and the notion of a router queue.
The trade-off analysis (reserved vs. on-demand bandwidth, wasted capacity during silent periods) presupposes knowledge of how circuits and FDM/TDM partition link capacity.
Packet loss is explained via finite queue capacity and is explicitly related to traffic intensity La/R approaching or exceeding 1, a quantity defined in the queuing-delay discussion.
The argument that packet switching suits bursty traffic rests on statistical multiplexing, and its drawbacks (queuing delay, packet loss under congestion) are key terms in the comparison.

The TCP/UDP discussion is an evaluation of the Internet's transport models against the four requirement classes (reliability, throughput, timing, security); the requirement classes must be defined first for the comparison and the SSL/TLS motivation to be meaningful.

The message-format discussion (7-bit ASCII restrictions of SMTP motivating MIME) builds directly on SMTP's command dialogue and its content restrictions; MIME is introduced as a response to SMTP's limitations.

Analyzing how HTTP uses TCP connections (one object per connection vs. multiple objects) and computing response times requires first understanding that HTTP is a stateless request-response protocol for fetching objects referenced by a web page.
HTTP/2's improvements (multiplexing, head-of-line blocking, page-load latency) are meaningful only against the baseline HTTP/1.x request-response model and the multi-object structure of web pages.
Understanding proxy servers, cache hits/misses, and serving HTTP requests on behalf of clients presupposes knowledge of the browser/server request-response model and web objects.
Cookies are explicitly presented as a mechanism for adding stateful user identification on top of HTTP's stateless model, so the stateless request-response model must be learned first.
Request lines, methods, status lines, and status codes only make sense once the student knows the HTTP client/server request-response model and what browsers ask of web servers.

Flow control relies on the receive window (rwnd) field carried in the TCP segment header; the sender reads this field to limit unacknowledged data.

Reliable data transfer is built on the 32-bit sequence and acknowledgment numbers (byte-stream offsets) and the ACK flag; cumulative acknowledgments cannot be understood without the segment's numbering scheme.

SampleRTT is measured by timing the transmission of a segment and receipt of its acknowledgment, which requires understanding sequence/acknowledgment numbers and the ACK flag defined in the segment structure.
The three-way handshake and teardown use the SYN, FIN, ACK, and RST header flags and involve sequence number selection, all defined in the segment structure.
rdt2.x builds directly on the rdt1.0 baseline by incrementally adding checksums, ACKs/NAKs, retransmissions, and sequence numbers to the same sender/receiver FSM framework.
Connection management details the lifecycle (handshake, state, teardown) of the connection abstraction; understanding why a handshake and per-connection state exist must come first.
The latency analysis of slow start explicitly motivates designs that determine the sending rate more quickly, which is exactly what the delay-based and ECN variants do.
The two control approaches are solutions to the congestion problem; understanding what congestion is and its costs (queuing delay, loss, collapse) is needed before classifying how to control it.

Classic TCP infers congestion from packet loss and growing delay; learners must first know that loss and queuing delay are the symptoms and costs of congestion that TCP reacts to. [expanded from sibling edge 'Causes and Costs of Congestion' -> 'Classic TCP Congestion Control']

Classic TCP is the canonical instance of end-to-end control (inferring congestion from loss/delay because IP provides no explicit feedback); the taxonomy is required to frame why TCP works the way it does. [expanded from sibling edge 'End-to-End vs. Network-Assisted Approaches' -> 'Classic TCP Congestion Control']

The newer variants are organized by this taxonomy: delay-based TCP is still end-to-end inference (via delay), while ECN is network-assisted explicit feedback; the approach distinction is needed to classify them.

TCP's congestion control (slow start, AIMD congestion avoidance, fast recovery) manipulates a congestion window alongside TCP's reliable data transfer, RTT estimation, and receive-window flow control; TCP's operation must be understood first for the congestion control mechanisms to make sense. [expanded from sibling edge 'Connection-Oriented Transport: TCP' -> 'Congestion Control']
Fast recovery implements the multiplicative-decrease step (halving cwnd on a triple duplicate-ACK loss) whose role in the AIMD cycle is defined in the congestion avoidance leaf.
The fairness convergence argument is a direct analysis of the additive-increase/multiplicative-decrease dynamics, so AIMD must be learned first.
SR is likewise a pipelined protocol whose design is motivated by the stop-and-wait utilization problem quantified in this analysis.
The poor utilization derived here is the explicit motivation for pipelined operation, which GBN implements via its sliding window of N outstanding packets.
rdt3.0 extends rdt2.2 by adding a countdown timer to handle lost packets; its duplicate-detection relies on the sequence-number machinery introduced in rdt2.x.
The utilization analysis quantifies the bandwidth waste of the completed stop-and-wait protocol (rdt3.0), using its sender behavior and RTT/L/R timing model.

Congestion avoidance begins when cwnd reaches the slow-start threshold (ssthresh) defined during slow start; the phase transition is a direct dependency.

AIMD's linear cwnd increase and multiplicative decrease on loss cannot be understood without first knowing what cwnd is and how loss (triple duplicate ACKs vs. timeout) is detected.
Slow start's exponential cwnd growth and its termination by ssthresh or a loss event presuppose the definitions of the congestion window and the loss signals introduced in this leaf.
Fast retransmit is triggered by three duplicate ACKs, which is one of the loss-signal distinctions (triple duplicate ACK vs. timeout) established in this leaf.
Flow control constrains the amount of unacknowledged (in-flight) data, a concept defined by the sender's acknowledgment and windowing behavior in reliable data transfer (LastByteSent, LastByteAcked).
The single retransmission timer's behavior, including timeout-triggered retransmissions and doubling the timeout, directly uses the TimeoutInterval computed from EstimatedRTT and DevRTT.

SDN controllers compute and distribute match+action flow tables, which are an instance of generalized forwarding, so generalized forwarding is a prerequisite.
Generalized forwarding extends the forwarding function beyond destination-based lookup, requiring the basic forwarding concept first.
Input/output port processing is the hardware realization of the per-router forwarding function, so the forwarding-vs-routing distinction must come first.
The switching fabric and queues are the internal mechanisms that accomplish forwarding within a router, which only makes sense once forwarding is defined.
Traditional IP forwarding details destination-based forwarding using the forwarding table, a concept introduced by the forwarding-vs-routing overview.
SDN explicitly separates the data plane from the control plane, which is precisely the forwarding/routing distinction, so that distinction is a direct prerequisite.
The switching fabric moves packets from input ports to output ports and queues form at those ports, so port operation must be understood first.
Generalized forwarding is defined in contrast to destination-based forwarding ('rather than the destination address alone'), so traditional forwarding must be learned first.

BGP is another instance of the distributed per-router control paradigm; the overview's taxonomy of per-router vs. SDN control provides the conceptual frame for why BGP computes and advertises routes among routers/ASes rather than via a central controller.

The SDN control plane topic elaborates the SDN approach defined in the overview; its controller/application architecture and separation of data and control planes presuppose familiarity with the SDN paradigm introduced there.

The overview establishes the per-router control paradigm in which routing algorithms run inside each router; OSPF is presented as an intra-AS instance of that approach, so the framing is needed to situate it.
OSPF implements link-state routing within an autonomous system, so understanding Dijkstra's least-cost computation and complete-topology link-state dissemination is a direct prerequisite.

BGP is a path-vector protocol that generalizes the distance-vector mechanism of iteratively exchanging reachability vectors with neighbors; the DV algorithm's distributed, iterative mechanics prepare students for BGP's AS-path advertisements.

Inter-AS routing presupposes the notion of autonomous systems with their own internal routing; BGP interconnects ASes whose intra-AS routing (e.g., OSPF) must be understood first to see how interior and exterior routes compose.

The comparison centers on how switches forward frames using MAC addresses and self-learning versus how routers forward datagrams; switch operation must be understood before contrasting it with routing.

Coverage distances of wireless standards are fundamentally limited by path loss, and transmission rates dropping with distance are a direct consequence of attenuation; path loss is needed to explain how rates and coverage vary with distance.

SNR is the ratio of received signal power to noise; understanding how attenuation and path loss reduce received power with distance is needed to explain why SNR falls and BER rises as sender-receiver distance grows.
